lines.text: Varr Keep stands on a bluff above the Senn, with black and gold banners on every tower. I grew up there. I hadn't been back since the day they sent me north.
We came in through the river gate at dusk. Five muddy strangers, a wolfhound and a beggar. The guards couldn't decide whether to bow or call for the dogs.
My father met us in the great hall. He didn't embrace me. He never had.
You got my letter.
A week late.
And you came anyway.
If I hadn't, they'd have hanged Halvard, and Ysolde, and every lord who signed for me. You'd have come too.
No. I would not.
He looked at Corvin the way he looked at mud on a carpet. Then he gave us rooms, and dry clothes, and dinner. And nothing else at all.
My brother came to dinner late. I almost didn't know him.
Maric had always been the handsome one. Now his face was thin, his eyes too bright, and his hands wouldn't keep still. A little glass vial hung at his throat, white as milk.
The famous zero. The boy who won Father's war with turnips. The hero of Kesting. They sing about you in the taverns, you know. Even here.
Nobody sings about me. Not since a drunk knocked me into the mud in front of the whole army.
Maric. What's in the vial?
The Order's draught. Medicine. They help loyal sons win back their name. You wouldn't understand. Nobody ever had to help you be nothing.
The silver cup in his hand had gone soft, and was dripping onto the tablecloth. He didn't notice. Father did. Father noticed, and looked away.
That night, I couldn't sleep. I'm always cold, and Varr Keep was colder than I remembered. So I walked.
In the great hall, my mother watched me from her portrait, as she always had. Lady Isolde Varr. Golden hair, and a cold, lovely face. She died the day I was born.
At the top of the old tower was a door that had been locked my whole childhood. Ash stopped in front of it, and whined.
Stewards learn every lock in a house, my lord. It's how we find out what the family is hiding.
Corvin had followed me, of course. It took him eleven heartbeats.
Inside, everything was under dust sheets. Except one painting, turned to face the wall.
I turned it round.
It wasn't Lady Isolde. It was a young woman with dark hair, in a plain grey dress, laughing at whoever was painting her.
She had my eyes.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter sixty-six, coming soon.
